items.title: Helen Oakley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: Rupert had died, that wonderful brother that Duke had loved too, and he died at Dieppe

ctx.x: Oh good. Well I’ll just tell you end of that then, because the end was I knew I was fighting a losing battle. Well then I put on a battle of the bands between Chick and Basie. And you knew that there was only one answer there. Although Chick, he was a battler. And of course the sound of his drums, there was nothing like it. And that bass, that boom boom, that started up, the whole Savoy Ballroom used to, lift the floor. And so Chick held his own as far as the people were concerned. But there was really no…

progressively dying. And so in Baltimore he went and played another thing on board ship, and we were in white, Baltimore, and he was making signals to me to get over and to speak and everything and I didn’t. Because I didn’t want to get him in trouble either. I mean I could have also been in trouble, and I didn’t want to get him in trouble, so I didn’t. And it broke my heart because he was giving me that eye, that desperate eye, and I didn’t. And he went straight into Johns Hopkins and died five days later. And…
I want to ask you a couple of things about those times. Chicago in the 30s, when you first started doing those records there, how was the depression and prohibition part of the whole atmosphere.
